courses.course_name: Technology Skills & Leadership in the 21st Century
courses.description: Students will learn both essential knowledge and applied skills to advance 21st Century Skills through authentic business projects, events, and conferences connected to involvement with the Future Business Leaders of America student organization. The curriculum will provide comprehensive strategies to prepare students with real life experiences and industry-specific technical skills before they attend college or enter the work force. Why do students need 21st Century Skills? “Every child in America needs to be ready for today’s and tomorrow’s world. A profound gap exists between the knowledge and skills most students learn in school and the knowledge and skills they need for success in their communities and workplaces. To successfully face rigorous higher education coursework, career challenges and a globally competitive workforce, U.S. schools must align classroom environments with real world environments by fusing the three Rs and four Cs (Critical thinking and problem solving, Communication, Collaboration, and Creativity and innovation skills).

courses.description: This course is designed to cover all the major functions of word processing. Students will learn to create documents, edit saved documents and print all documents. Some features that will be covered are spell check, tables, merge/sort documents, forms, outlines, and graphics. FINAL EXAM will be a Microsoft Office Specialist (MOS) test simulation. Students will be given the opportunity to obtain MOS certification.

This course is designed for the student to learn about spreadsheet software application. Spreadsheets are used for analyzing, managing and presenting information. All basic functions will be covered in this course including some database and graphic applications. FINAL EXAM will be a Microsoft Office Specialist (MOS) test simulation. Students will be given the opportunity to obtain MOS certification.

This course is designed for the student to learn about database software application. Databases are collections of related information. Once you have created a database, a student will be able to sort it, search for particular items, and prepare reports that show particular aspects of the data. All basic functions will be covered in this course. FINAL EXAM will be a Microsoft Office Specialist (MOS) test simulation. Students will be given the opportunity to obtain MOS certification.

This course will teach students how to create various presentations using slides, outlines, speaker’s notes, and audience handouts. Presentations can include text, clip art, graphs, tables, charts, and even sound or video clips. FINAL EXAM will be a Microsoft Office Specialist (MOS) test simulation. Students will be given the opportunity to obtain MOS certification.

A hands-on introduction to information processing using operating system and application software designed for computers and mobile devices. Covers file management, presentation graphics, word processing, and spreadsheets. Basic algebra skills are recommended.

Students will acquire skills required for competency in beginning accounting and will serve as an introduction to the accounting field. The course includes the preparation and interpretation of financial statements and other business data. Students will have the option of using traditional or online text and will be using online working papers to provide instant feedback through automated assessments.

courses.course_name: Programming for the Web in HTML
courses.description: There is no prerequisite for this course. Students enrolled in this course will learn HyperText Markup Language (HTML), the universal code that structures and defines online content. Through hands-on coding projects, students will gain real-world skills for building the framework of websites, applications, emails, and more. Leveraging HTML elements and attributes, students will learn how to format text, insert media, create forms, link pages, deploy sites, and use best practices. Upon completion, students will have a portfolio of hand-coded web pages demonstrating mastery of clean, semantic HTML code. This course develops essential knowledge for anyone publishing content online or pursuing careers in web development.

courses.course_name: Programming for the Web in CSS
courses.description: Students enrolled in this course will learn Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) - the essential language for visually styling web pages and online content. Through hands-on coding projects, students will gain real-world skills for turning plain HTML sites into fully designed, professional web pages that grab attention. Leveraging their knowledge of HTML, students will learn how to format text, customize colors and fonts, craft responsive page layouts, incorporate media like video/audio, animate page elements, and deploy across devices. Upon completion, students will have a portfolio of stylish, modern web pages showcasing mastery over text, content, and overall presentation using CSS. This course develops essential skills for publishing any online content or launching web development careers.

courses.course_name: Programming for the Web in JavaScript
courses.description: In this course, students will immerse themselves in the art and science of JavaScript programming. JavaScript, the dynamic language that powers modern web applications, is at the heart of user interactivity and real-time content updates. Through a rigorous curriculum, students will not only master the syntax but also explore the deeper principles of problem-solving and creative design. The course objectives include understanding the transformative role of JavaScript in turning static web pages into dynamic, responsive interfaces. From form validation to interactive applications, students will harness JavaScript’s power to create seamless user experiences. Additionally, students will move beyond surface-level coding, diving into event-driven programming, asynchronous operations, and best practices. Along the way, they’ll craft small-scale applications, such as calculators and games, while honing their analytical skills. For aspiring programmers and computer scientists, JavaScript proficiency is non-negotiable. This course lays the groundwork for future endeavors in web development, software engineering, and data science.
courses.prerequisites: Programming for the Web in HTML

courses.course_name: Programming for the Web in PHP
courses.description: Students enrolled in this course will learn server-side web programming using PHP, the popular open-source language used by elite web developers. Through hands-on projects, students will build dynamic web applications like e-commerce sites, blogs, content management systems, and more. Leveraging their existing knowledge of HTML, CSS and JavaScript, students will learn how to integrate backend databases, process form data, manage sessions and cookies, implement login systems, and connect to APIs. This course prepares students for web development careers or computer science majors.
courses.prerequisites: Programming for the Web in HTML

courses.description: This course blends challenging C++ programming with intricate electronic wiring using Arduino microcontrollers and components like sensors, motors, and LEDs. Designed for students comfortable with iterating designs, it fuses creativity with technical precision as students meticulously build and program robots that push the boundaries of innovation. The course is geared for individuals who thrive when solving complex problems through diligent work and independent practice. It aims to hone programming skills and unlock the fascinating world of electronics integration.

This course introduces Blender - the powerful open-source tool used by animators, game designers and 3D artists worldwide to bring imaginative worlds to life. Through hands-on modeling projects, students will learn the foundations of computer-generated 3D art, from manipulating 3D meshes to texturing, lighting, rigging animations, and rendering photoreal visuals. Explore Blender’s exceptional animation toolset while bringing characters, creatures, props, concepts and architectures to fruition. Portfolios of student projects will showcase talents to prospective colleges or future employers in arts, film, gaming, and more. For those with an inventive spark, unlock your 3D imagination with Blender!

Each phase has its own special values. In the classroom, learning activities cover the entire scope of Traffic Safety Education, not only knowledge of physical control of the car but conditions that influence the driving task. In-car is an application of the driving practices, laws, visual techniques and skills needed to pass your state driving exam.

courses.description: Through careful study of classic and contemporary texts from around the world in multiple genres, students will explore how great authors have approached key thematic ideas that touch us all. Throughout history and across the globe, great writers have consistently been drawn to explore what it means to be human—the nature of friendship, the roots of identity, the grip of fear, the force of desire, the power of love and of hate. With a focus on close reading, academic writing, and literary analysis, this course will study how great writers use both similar and various techniques to communicate important truths about human nature and the human experience. Course materials are tied to units of study in the World History curriculum.

courses.description: Humanities is an English class for ninth graders that offers instruction in reading, writing, speaking and listening, and language development (grammar study and vocabulary acquisition). The English curriculum runs parallel to the Social Studies curriculum in ninth grade; units address world history from the Renaissance to the present, and students read literature from across the globe. Reading instruction focuses on the development of fluency, comprehension, and vocabulary through the careful, close reading of both fiction and non-fiction sources. Students build vocabulary, learn reading and study strategies, and use the writing process to develop clear, thoughtful, multi-paragraph essays in response to their reading. Research is also a component of Humanities. Students have multiple opportunities to develop each of the school’s Learning Expectations through a variety of Folio Tasks tied to the course content.

Students will be expected to read several novels, plays, short stories and poems in the American literary canon; to write a variety of essays, stories and poems; to create artistic representations of thematic material; and to actively engage in class discussion of the course content. Students produce several formal essays, including a biography and synthesis writing, write short stories and poetry, and conduct research.

courses.description: Composition is an academic writing course focused on argument writing. In this course, students will research, discuss, analyze, and write persuasively about important and controversial societal issues. Students will work on understanding nuance and complexity, keeping an open mind, and acknowledging the validity of competing viewpoints. After looking closely at a wide range of evidence and perspectives from multiple sources, students will arrive at their own informed conclusions about a topic and construct argument essays that organize and synthesize evidence to support those conclusions. As this cycle gets repeated for different topics, students will strengthen skills relating to reading informational text, locating quality sources, citing evidence, analyzing and describing data, elaboration, writing with effective organization, and revision.

courses.description: Students in this writing workshop course will build essential writing skills through several styles and purposes of writing. In personal writing, students will develop descriptive and reflective skills to share the story of a meaningful experience. In informative and argumentative writing, students will organize ideas and information to clearly communicate their knowledge of and support their opinions on multiple topics. We will also spend a fair amount of time mastering the kind of writing that often accompanies college and job applications (resumes, cover letters, statements of purpose etc.). Study of grammar, usage, and the mechanics of writing will be embedded throughout the semester as needed. Students will grow as writers through the sometimes messy and frustrating but also rewarding stages of the writing process: reading, thinking, discussing, drafting, receiving feedback, reconsidering, revising, editing, and publishing.

courses.description: What does it take to survive in a hostile environment? What are the physical and emotional resources that promote survival in difficult circumstances? These are just two of the questions students will explore in Survival Stories, a course that examines what it takes to thrive in trying times (in history) or in challenging environments (the natural world). Note: The particular focus of this class will depend on student interest, and students will have opportunities to choose their own survival stories to read.
courses.notes: Elective Program (grades 11-12): one-term, half-credit classes; some classes may not be offered every year.

courses.description: Students will read war stories through the lens of the American experience of armed conflict. They will read accounts of war from a variety of perspectives, including those of combatants and those of noncombatants affected by the conflict. Reading materials for this course will include fiction and non-fiction texts as well as recent films. The goal is to engage students in a thoughtful consideration of conflict and its impact on the people involved.
courses.notes: Elective Program (grades 11-12): one-term, half-credit classes; some classes may not be offered every year.

There are lessons to help students explore the songs. The purpose of the course is to develop students’ reading, writing, and discussion skills.

courses.description: This one-term course will survey the writing of Vermonters with a special focus on the literature of the Northeast Kingdom. It will illuminate the history and heritage of the state, sampling literature from the turn of the century to the present day. Representative authors include James Hayford, Robert Frost, E. Annie Proulx, David Budbill, and Howard Frank Mosher, among others. Student participation in class discussion and individual projects is required;reading assignments will be many and various.

courses.description: This course explores the craft of fiction in some favorite types of modern literature. Genres that may be examined include horror, fantasy, science fiction, satire, regional literature, mystery, memoir and humor in short story or book length. Films and outside readings will supplement this review of the genres, as will both formal and informal writing activities.
courses.notes: Elective Program (grades 11-12): one-term, half-credit classes; some classes may not be offered every year.

courses.description: In this course we will explore the role of storytelling in civilization and humanity's quest for knowledge of self. We will explore ancient Creation Myths that have endured for centuries, shaping cultures around the world and students will have the opportunity to write their own Creation Myths. We will dive into The "Hero's Journey" formula and focus will be on the Gods and Goddesses and Creatures of Greek Mythology. We will read a novel that weaves in many of the Greek Myths in a contemporary storyline and students will try their hand at writing their own "Hero's Journey" story.
courses.notes: Elective Program (grades 11-12): one-term, half-credit classes; some classes may not be offered every year.

courses.description: Graphic novels are finally being recognized as great literature. Graphic novels explore the complex themes that touch us all—violence, fear, love, mental health, addiction, friendship, betrayal, and more. This class will explore how authors and artists tell stories using a new and exciting form—the graphic novel—while still relying heavily on traditional storytelling techniques. Along the way, we will read some of the most respected and exciting works in the genre, such as Watchmen, I Kill Giants, V for Vendetta, American Born Chinese, and more. Specific texts subject to change.
courses.notes: Elective Program (grades 11-12): one-term, half-credit classes; some classes may not be offered every year.

courses.description: Some people fall apart when faced with horrible things. Others rise above and fight back. In this class, we will study how authors explore human nature through stories of horror and apocalypse (the end of the world as we know it). Horror can be realistic or wildly imaginative; it can focus on human madness or inhuman monsters; it can tell the story of a single lost child or a massive global catastrophe. In any case, ‘horrible’ stories force us to take a hard look at ourselves and those around us. This is because authors often explore the darker side of humans and the terrible things we are capable of. At the same time, these same stories expose the resilience and kindness of characters determined to survive, reminding us of the strength we all have within us.
courses.notes: Elective Program (grades 11-12): one-term, half-credit classes; some classes may not be offered every year.

courses.description: From the farthest reaches of space to the aliens in our own backyards, science fiction stories ask us to stretch the boundaries of what is possible. In this course, students will be asked to examine how science fiction authors create fantastical stories that ask the question our everyday world can’t: “what if?” While creative, stories of the science fiction genre get to the harsh truths of reality around us, asking us to think critically about our own lives and society itself. In this course, students will analyze a variety of sci-fi stories from some of the greats – (Ray Bradbury, Roald Dahl, Kurt Vonnegut, Aldous Huxley) before creating a short story of their own. With each story, students will also research and analyze how parts of their own life connect directly to the elaborate worlds of science fiction.
courses.notes: Elective Program (grades 11-12): one-term, half-credit classes; some classes may not be offered every year.

courses.description: Written words are everywhere. In addition to old trusty books, words show up on road signs, food labels, twitter feeds, news articles, text messages, internet memes, magazines, and blogs. In all situations, someone put those words there to communicate ideas, information, emotions, opinions, and perspectives. In this course, students will carefully and creatively examine and experience the astounding variety of ways that words tell stories. We will conduct this exploration by reading examples of high quality fiction, non-fiction, and poetry to serve as models for writing. Students will develop the skills of perception and description through language – skills that make for great writing and help us live more thoughtfully and perceptively. Much of the writing done in the course will be shared during class workshops and published to the wider school.

With nonfiction movies, it is on how the filmmaker has communicated a viewpoint. Movies studied in recent years include: Rocky, The Sting, Murderball, Restrepo, Undefeated, Gleason, Heart of the Game, and For Sam. Note: Some of the movies in the course are rated “R” or are unrated, and parental permission will be required for students to watch them.

The reading is challenging, college-level material. Students also write numerous essays, mostly of two types: (1) argumentative essays, and (2) essays that attempt to explain how a piece of writing is effective. Students also prepare for the national AP Language & Composition exam, which consists of both essay writing and multiple-choice reading questions.

Upon successful completion of an Advanced Placement College Board exam, a student may receive college credit and appropriate placement in participating colleges.

Concert selections will include music from a wide variety of cultural and historical genres. Participation in school concerts is mandatory. Chorus members are eligible to participate in the Northeast VT District II Music Festival.

The focus of the class is Jazz, but students will also work on classical repertoire and modern band (contemporary commercial music such as blues, rock, pop, etc.). Singers are welcome to take this class but will need to play an instrument as well as sing. The program is dynamic and flexible, with a focus on live performance and festivals. In addition to required concerts, students will receive opportunities for community service through performances. Content covered includes instrumental techniques, tuning and intonation, scales, rhythmic studies, note identification, arranging, composition and written music theory. Playing more than one instrument is encouraged. Rhythm section players and all levels, including beginners, are welcome.

courses.description: This class will trace the history of rock music from the blues to the present day. Genres include blues and folk, rock, rockabilly, country, rock and roll, the British invasion, alternative, metal and punk. Students will reflect and critique these musical styles using discipline specific vocabulary, read articles about the various genres, and learn to identify these genres aurally. Students will study how rock music has been associated with political activism as well as changes in social attitudes, and is often seen as an expression of youth revolt against adult conformity.

courses.description: This course is for students who love to sing. The primary focus of the class is to build a healthy and free singing voice. Students will select a classical, popular or jazz solo and participate in several a capella projects, either classical, folk or world music. Music theory concepts will be taught as they apply to specific examples of song literature, including solfege, key signatures, rhythmic studies and the elements of music (music terminology). Students will be prepared for auditions and performances. (District 2 Jazz, Northeast Rotary Festival, All-State Music Festival and New England Music Festivals). If you are in chorus or want to strengthen your singing voice for the school musical, this is the perfect class for you.
courses.notes: Music. Can be repeated for credit. No prerequisite. Listed in Course Summary without a course number.

courses.description: This course is for singers who wish to enhance their ability to read printed music and to sing in parts. The curriculum includes keyboard skills, written theory, solfege and rhythmic sight reading and analysis. Students will choose solo and ensemble projects from the classical, jazz, folk and world music genres. Students will be prepared for auditions and performances. (District 2 Jazz, Northeast Rotary Festival, All-State Music Festival and New England Music Festivals). If you are interested in being fluent in conventional music notation, developing keyboard skills and analyzing music, this class is for you. Music Theory for Singers is also an excellent preparatory class for AP Music Theory or if you are considering a music major or minor in college. There are four levels in the class, so this can be repeated for credit and there is no prerequisite.
courses.prerequisites: None, although this course is most effective when taken concurrently with Chorus. This course is highly recommended for singers who wish to audition for the Northeast, All-State, and All-New England Music Festivals, and for singers not in band who are considering a career in music.
courses.notes: Music. There are four levels in the class and it can be repeated for credit.

courses.description: A major component of any college preparatory curriculum in music is a course introducing the first-year student to music theory, a subject that comprises the musical materials and procedures of the Common Practice period. AP Music Theory integrates aspects of melody, harmony, texture, rhythm, form, musical analysis, elementary composition, and to some extent, history and style. Musicianship skills such as dictation, sight-singing, and keyboard harmony are also a part of this course. The student’s ability to read and write musical notation is fundamental. It is also assumed that the student has acquired (or is acquiring) at least basic performance skills in voice or on an instrument. Possibility for college credit upon successful completion of AP Music Theory Exam.

Students will learn how to use camera functions and settings, as well as photographic manipulation techniques in Adobe Photoshop to produce successful photographs.

Students who enter this course must have taken a semester of both two-dimensional art and three-dimensional art. With this art foundation, we are able to explore techniques and ideas beyond what is covered in the introductory classes. Students will also prepare a portfolio of their work for college entrance.

courses.description: This course is a review of the operations on whole numbers, fractions, decimals, and percentages and related problems. Geometry, measurement, and probability are also covered.
This course is a continuation of Essentials of Mathematics I. Essentials II emphasizes life skills such as banking, budget planning, insurance, taxes, and personal planning.

Pre-Algebra gives a preliminary introduction to the concepts of algebra while providing the student with the opportunity to improve his/her skills in core mathematical areas. Topics covered in this course include fractions, decimals and percentages as well as patterns, operations with integers, graphs, probability, introduction to variables and algebraic concepts.

Consumer Mathematics is designed as a third year offering for those completing Essentials of Mathematics II. The fundamental operations of whole numbers, fractions, decimals, and percentages are used to solve problems which are intrinsic to everyday life. These problems may include sales, computing interest, and budgeting.

Algebra 1 introduces students to variables, algebraic expressions, equations, inequalities, functions, and all their multiple representations. In this class, students will develop the ability to explore and solve real-world application problems, demonstrate the appropriate use of graphing calculators, and communicate mathematical ideas clearly. Time permitting, quadratic equations will be introduced and solved using both the factoring and quadratic formula methods. This course lays the foundation for mathematical literacy that will help students be successful in every subsequent course in mathematics.

This course is designed for the student who has excelled in junior high mathematics. It is a faster paced course which covers more ground and delves more deeply into some of the algebra concepts than does the regular course. Graphing calculators will be used more extensively than in the regular Algebra I course.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation and permission from the teacher of record.

courses.description: Students in this course will explore such concepts of geometry as symmetry, congruence, and similarity as well as receive an introduction to logic. Students will use both inductive and deductive reasoning to prove statements about congruent and similar triangles, parallel lines, polygons, and circles. Properties of right triangles including the Pythagorean Theorem are studied. Area and volumes of planar and solid figures are calculated. Transformations of figures are studied. Problem solving is integrated throughout the course.

This course will cover the same concepts and content as Geometry 40105. The course will be offered in the summer and will also require extensive independent work completion, as well as work with the instructor during Semester One for credit. This course will only be run if a minimum of 15 students enroll. See your guidance counselor for specific dates and times.
courses.offering_note: Offered in the summer; will only be run if a minimum of 15 students enroll
courses.notes: Course Summary prerequisite: Sophomore standing.

courses.description: This course is designed for the student who has excelled in Algebra I and is intending to continue through four years of mathematics. It is a faster paced course which covers more ground and delves more deeply into some of the geometry concepts than the regular course does.
courses.prerequisites: Honors Algebra I with a grade of B or above, or permission.

courses.description: This course is a continuation of the concepts developed in Algebra I and Geometry. Topics covered include: Linear equations, functions, solving systems of linear equations and inequalities, matrices and determinants, quadratic functions, polynomials, factoring, radicals, exponential and logarithmic functions, and possibly trigonometric functions, sequences and series as time permits.

This course is designed for the student who excels in mathematics and sees a possible career in the field of mathematics or science. It is a faster paced course than Algebra II, and graphing calculators are used more extensively.
courses.prerequisites: Honors Geometry with a grade of B or above, or permission.

courses.description: This course is designed to review and enhance Algebra and Geometry skills through a variety of real life applications and problem-solving. This course also covers general Pre-Calculus topics

This course’s fundamental units of study are centered on managing one’s money, spending wisely, making money grow and basic business mathematics analysis. Within these units, students will study about checking and savings accounts and budgeting. Income taxes, insurance options, credit card management, and basic investment options are also covered. The use of Excel spreadsheet with formulas is emphasized.

Honors Pre-Calculus is a rigorous course involving a thorough investigation of numerous and varied mathematical concepts to fully prepare students for the study of calculus. Beginning with a review of functions (linear, quadratic, polynomial, rational, logarithmic, exponential, inverse), the course concludes with a study of trigonometry including the unit circle and graphs of trigonometric functions, trigonometric equations, and double and half angles.
courses.prerequisites: Honors Algebra II with a grade of B or above, or grade of an A in Algebra II and teacher recommendation.

courses.description: This college level course will explore such topics as experiments, data collection, data analysis, averages & variation, probability, normal distributions, sampling distributions, estimation, hypothesis testing, regression, correlation, and chi-square distributions. Upon successful completion of this course, students who have completed the two semester statistics sequence may opt to take the AP Statistics exam to earn college credit.

Calculus is an advanced placement course in which the student may receive college credit upon successful completion of an examination. The course begins with a quick review of elementary functions. This includes the properties and graphs of algebraic, exponential, logarithmic, & trigonometric functions. Limits and continuity of functions are discussed and related to derivatives of functions; applications of the derivatives such as curve sketching and extreme value problems are taught. Techniques of integration and applications of the integral, which include area between curves and volumes of solids, are also presented. Graphing calculators are used extensively in this course.
courses.prerequisites: Pre-Calculus and permission from the teacher of record.

courses.description: Freshman PE will cover a wide variety of activities including fitness, team sports, and individual/net sports. This class will act as an introduction to each of the class offerings that students will have the choice to take later on as upper classmen at Lake Region. Each unit covered will provide students with multiple opportunities to become proficient in the core skills and techniques to be successful in later PE classes.

This is a required semester course that will be completed in the freshman year. Students will engage in activities and assignments that assess and analyze their own personal habits in nutrition, fitness, and mental health. They will choose health-related topics to research, learn some basic first aid skills, practice effective communication skills, and discuss stress management. Students will practice problem-solving and conflict resolution techniques, identify body organs and functions, and understand the aging process. They will learn about disease prevention through lifestyle choices and identify factors that can contribute to poor health, including those related to sexual health and substances. The focus is on developing and maintaining healthy lifestyles through personal skills and responsibility.
courses.fulfills_text: This is a required semester course that will be completed in the freshman year.

courses.description: Fitness/weightlifting will offer students the opportunity to create and implement a term long fitness plan based on goals created in the beginning week of the class. Students with no weightlifting experience are encouraged to take this class and learn a lifestyle to promote health and fitness. This class will be mostly centered around the LR weightlifting and cardio facility, but at times may use other spaces (gym, outside) in order to offer students a wide variety of fitness activities. Lastly, this class will act as an introduction to exercise science and cover how physical activity affects our bodies; students will learn the basics of anatomy and physiology as well.
courses.notes: Prerequisite from Course Summary.

courses.description: Team sports will offer students the opportunity to participate in a wide variety of team sports with their fellow classmates. This class requires teamwork and communication skills to be successful. Some of the units covered include but are not limited to ultimate frisbee, flag football, floor hockey, handball/speedball, lacrosse, softball/wiffle ball, and basketball.
courses.notes: Prerequisite from Course Summary.

courses.description: Individual/net sports will offer students a wide variety of activities to participate in individually, or in small groups. This class will help students explore lifelong sporting activities they can participate in without a team. Some of the units covered include but are not limited to orienteering, golf, disc golf, pickle ball, badminton, cross country skiing, snowshoeing, tennis, and archery.
courses.notes: Prerequisite from Course Summary.

courses.description: Personal Wellness is an elective semester course that combines wellness with independent living skills. It is a project based class that includes financial literacy, professionalism, life skills, emotional and social health, mindfulness, nutrition and meal planning, self-care, complementary therapies, hobbies, environmentally healthy living, with fitness activities one day a week. Students develop resumes and cover letters, research and analyze car and home expenses, plan healthy meals and shopping lists, create budgets, and practice interview skills. They also learn a breadth of healthy lifestyle habits that promote physical and mental well-being.

This elective is for students who may be interested in a career in healthcare, education, or social services and want to learn more about human growth and development and nutrition. Students will research and compare public service careers. They will study the physical, emotional, social, and cognitive changes throughout the various stages of human development. Students will analyze factors that influence food choices and understand how nutrition impacts various areas of health. Each student will choose a specific population or age group to focus on, research local and global needs and develop strategies to address those concerns.

Educational practices will include questioning and problem solving, modeling, investigations requiring data collection and computation, independent technical research, and communication of critical issues facing the planet.

Earth’s place in the Universe, Weather and Climate, Earth’s Interior, Energy and Matter, and Human Impacts are some of the topics explored through a variety of classroom and take-home work experiences.

Land, Air, Water and Space will be investigated with both global and local perspectives. Learning experiences will require communication and collaboration, while emphasizing independent skill building.

courses.description: This rigorous course is guided by the Next Generation Science Standards and is an in-depth exploration of the living world. The course is divided into four major units: Ecology, Cellular Biology, Genetics and Evolution. Life will be explored at different scales of complexity from molecules to ecosystems. Students will come to understand the patterns of interactions at these different scales and will investigate the interconnectedness of the living and nonliving world. Students will be challenged by individual and collaborative projects and labs which will build skills in organization, observation, data collection and analysis.

Building skills in organization, observation, data collection, analysis and conclusions is an essential part of making this course relative to real life experience and current scientific issues. Group work and individual projects are devised to challenge and engage students in a higher level of understanding of the cell, bacteria, protists, viruses, and classification. Students are evaluated on their notebooks, test scores, lab write-ups, homework and projects.

courses.description: Choose This Course If… your future plans include any type of college-level science or engineering coursework OR if you are just interested in science and enjoy a challenge! Overview: This is a rigorous science course designed to prepare students for introductory college science courses. There will be a strong emphasis on exploring topics both mathematically and conceptually, with hands-on labs accompanying most topics. Labs range from short guided activities to longer student-designed experiments and/or projects requiring lab reports and/or presentations. Students are expected to come into the course with strong study skills, fluency with basic algebra, and an eagerness to learn challenging content both within a supportive classroom community during class time and through regular homework. Students will work primarily in small permanent teams and are expected to develop their collaboration and leadership skills throughout the course. Topics Covered: 1) Basics of Matter & the Nature of Science, 2) Atoms & Quantum Theory, 3) the Periodic Table, Periodicity, & Chemical Bonding, 4) Chemical Reactions & Stoichiometry, 5) Thermochemistry & Gas Laws, and 6) Solutions, Kinetics, & Equilibrium. If time permits, additional topics, such as Nuclear Chemistry, Acids & Bases, Organic Chemistry, and/or Materials Science may be covered as well.
courses.prerequisites: A strong grasp of Algebra and Honors Biology or department approval

courses.description: Choose This Course If… you are interested in learning more about science and the world but are not necessarily planning to study science or engineering in college (or go to college at all). Overview: Unlike Honors Chemistry, this course is primarily designed to help students develop a deeper understanding of the physical world around them and the ability to apply scientific thinking to current real world problems, rather than focusing on preparation for college science. There is focus on conceptual understanding as well as making connections between scientific concepts, real world phenomena, and ethics, culture, and public policy. Frequent hands-on activities will accompany most topics, ranging from guided activities to student-designed labs and/or projects involving debates and/or presentations. Students will work in permanent teams and are expected to develop their collaboration and leadership skills throughout the course. Lessons are largely discussion and lab-based, so attendance and engagement during class are both critical for success. Topics Covered: 1) Searching for Life in Space (matter, atoms, quantum theory, bonding, light, the periodic table), 2) Fuels & CO2 (chemical reactions, moles, thermochemistry, gases), and 3) Ocean Acidification & Shellfish (acids & bases, reaction rates, equilibrium, solutions). If time permits, additional topics including Nuclear Chemistry, Polar Ice & Sea-Level Rise, Organic Chemistry, and/or Materials Science may be covered as well.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I, Earth Science and Biology

courses.description: This course is a study of the structure and function of the human body. This class addresses the inner workings of the human body through the study of body systems. There will be an emphasis on how the structure of cells, tissues, organs and organ systems relates to their respective functions. Throughout the course, a number of body systems will be addressed which will include many of the following: Integumentary, Skeletal, Muscular, Digestive, Circulatory, Respiratory, Nervous, Endocrine, Lymphatic, Immune and Reproductive Systems. This is an important course for anyone considering a career in health sciences.

Physics is the study of the rules and laws of the physical world. Much of the course is dedicated to using logic to understand physical systems. Topics may vary but will include basic mechanics. Science and math will intersect in laboratory experiments and group projects and will help to support an understanding of the physical world. This course is designed for curious juniors and seniors who have a strong mathematical background.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion, or current enrollment in Algebra II

courses.course_name: Locavore Science: Cheese, Bread, and Fermentation
courses.description: This course will study the biological foundations of the making and production of these three specific local food products: cheese, bread, and fermented items. Students will investigate the process with hands-on labs in the class regarding each food item. The follow-up to the science of making these products may include a visit to a local processing center that focuses on these products. Students will be quizzed and graded on the science of these products and given Portfolio tasks for the research, development, and communication involved in the future of these products as businesses in the Northeast Kingdom.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Biology and Algebra I

courses.description: This interdisciplinary course is designed for motivated Juniors and Seniors looking to learn more about the most pressing and urgent issue facing humankind, Climate Change, for which today’s youth will be forced to find global and local solutions. Students will be challenged to learn how Chemistry, Physics, Earth Science, and Biology all intersect. The course will explore the basic science behind climate, as well as the role technology plays in both the problems and possible solutions to the Climate Crisis. Students will participate in hands-on labs, analyze data, model complex systems, and learn how they can be part of local, state, national, and global solutions to this crisis beyond just recycling and turning the heat down!
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Biology and Algebra I

courses.description: This science class explores the application of scientific principles, primarily from Biology and Chemistry, to analyze and interpret evidence found at crime scenes. These could include the use of techniques like fingerprint analysis, DNA profiling, blood typing, fiber analysis, ballistics, and trace evidence collecting while emphasizing proper crime scene investigative procedures. Also included are critical thinking skills to solve simulated criminal cases. Students will engage in hands-on laboratory activities to practice these techniques and develop an understanding of the legal system’s role in forensics science.

courses.description: AP Physics I is a rigorous, college-level, algebra-based course that covers mechanics. Students will learn how to apply algebra and trigonometry to physical systems in order to understand how the universe works on a fundamental level. Students will be expected to engage with difficult classwork, complete frequent inquiry-based lab activities, and handle a consistent homework load. Students should enjoy challenges and bring strong study, math, collaboration, and computer skills to their work. Students should plan on taking the AP Physics I (Algebra-Based) exam in May.
courses.prerequisites: Success in Honors Algebra II (completion of Pre-Calculus and concurrent enrollment in Calculus recommended) or department approval

courses.description: Advanced Placement Biology is a college-level course introducing students to principles and processes of biology on a molecular level. Students cultivate their understanding of biology through inquiry-based investigations as they explore the following topics: biochemistry, cellular biology, energetics, communication, genetics, evolution, and ecology. The class focuses on laboratory experiences and hands-on experiences to provide students with the opportunity to apply the science practices. Students will be prepared for and may choose to take the AP Biology exam in May.

courses.description: Global Citizenship is structured upon the Inquiry process learned in the 9th and 10 grades, providing students the opportunity to engage in independent research on social issues of their own choosing. Students will experience a structured curriculum regarding citizenship, including the following topics: Recent History of the ‘70s to Today, Social Science Methodology, Identity & Culture, Social Institutions & Organization, Social Inequality, Economic Inequality, Sustainability and Citizenship & Social Change.

Scientific analysis of each student’s own field of research will be emphasized. Outside reading and study are essential requirements of this course. An emphasis will be placed on preparing students to be successful on both the AP Psychology exam as well as in college course.
courses.notes: Grade 11 & 12 Advanced Placement Program. Notes: Students must take two APs to meet the Global Citizenship graduation requirements. Prerequisite from Course Summary.

courses.description: The course curriculum encompasses the systematic study of patterns and processes that have shaped human understanding, use, and alteration of Earth's surface. Students examine human social organization and its environmental consequences. They also learn about the methods and tools geographers use in their science and practice. The units in the course focus on topics including thinking geographically, population and migration, culture, political geography, agriculture, urban geography, and development and industrialization. Students will have multiple opportunities to apply the information addressed in each unit in activities including note-taking, current events, projects, and formative and summative assessments. If students have not taken AP US Government and Politics, to fulfill the US Citizenship portion of Global Citizenship graduation standards, students must engage in an additional unit of study after the AP exam that is not part of the College Board curriculum.

courses.description: AP U.S. Government and Politics provides a college-level, nonpartisan introduction to key political concepts, ideas, institutions, policies, interactions, roles, and behaviors that characterize the constitutional system and political culture of the United States. Students will study U.S. foundational documents, Supreme Court decisions, and other texts and visuals to gain an understanding of the relationships and interactions among political institutions, processes, and behaviors. They will also engage in disciplinary practices that require them to read and interpret data, make comparisons and applications, and develop evidence-based arguments (College Board, 2020). The course is developed by the College Board, and has been endorsed by the National Constitution Center, a non-partisan, private foundation whose mission is to “disseminate information about the US Constitution (College Board, 2020).”

courses.description: This introductory CAD course teaches students professional 2D drawing techniques for drafting precise technical sketches. Through hands-on projects using industry-standard CAD software, students will develop skills to visualize, layout, dimension, and annotate technical drawings. Leveraging math skills including fractions, decimals and geometry, students will learn orthographic projection, isometric views and design conventions needed to draft accurate diagrams, blueprints, and schematics. The 2D CAD skills honed in this course build an essential foundation for professional engineering and design careers spanning manufacturing, construction, robotics and beyond

courses.description: In this course, students will elevate their 2D CAD drafting skills to the next level by mastering 3D modeling. Using industry-leading CAD software, participants will learn to transform technical drawings into intricate 3D models. From mechanical designs to architectural structures, attention to detail is paramount. Mathematical concepts, including fractions, decimals, and geometry, will be leveraged to create and manipulate realistic 3D forms. Additionally, students will explore the entire workflow, including model preparation and 3D printing techniques. By acquiring real-world 3D modeling expertise, students gain a competitive edge in STEM and technical fields, from robotics to manufacturing.

courses.description: This hands-on course explores alternative energy, conservation of resources and green building practices. Students will gain experience in these areas by researching, building, creating and evaluating projects they create. They will explore Electricity, Photovoltaic Solar panel design, Passive solar oven design, Hot water solar design, Biofuels, Hydroelectric Power, Wind turbine design, Green building construction practices, Hydrogen fuel cells and electric powered vehicles. As time will allow, we will visit a wind farm, solar field, hydroelectric power station, and a methane digester.

courses.description: This course is designed to give students experience in the creative art of woodworking and cabinetmaking. Students will explore all aspects of woodworking, from reading blueprints and measuring with accuracy, to creating wooden joints and inlays. They will learn how to safely use hand and power tools commonly used in the woodshop. They will learn about different types of wood and how they can be used in the woodworking process. Students will create a variety of wood projects, each building on the experience gained from the previous project. Students will also learn state of the art CNC or computer controlled woodworking.

courses.description: Students will explore many aspects of plant science. Horticulture is the study of plants. Students will explore plant identification, plant nutrition, soil composition, fertilizers and plant diseases. Students will create floral arrangements, terrariums, hydroponics systems, Bonsai trees, and more. Greenhouse operation is applying horticultural practices into an artificial environment. Students will explore types of greenhouses, setting up a greenhouse, artificial lighting, temperature control, proper water application, and fertilization in preparation for their annual plant sale. Students will be learning and doing different types of tree grafting. Students will start and grow seeds and plants in the Lake Region greenhouse environment. If time allows, students will visit commercial nurseries and the Montreal Botanical gardens.

We will explore four main types of welding: mig, stick, tig, and aluminum.

courses.description: This course is an introduction to the French language as it is currently used in Europe, the Americas and throughout the world. Students can expect to listen, speak, read and write within a broad cultural context. The student should also expect to engage in daily conversation in the target language. Awareness, understanding and respect of other cultures and their diversity are in integral part of this course. Skills to be acquired include: conjugate a verb in the present tense; understand adjective agreement, syntax of basic declarative sentences and interrogative sentences; recognize the phonics of the language; respond to basic questions; make comparisons. Vocabulary: numbers; family; politeness; time qualifiers; travel vocabulary; food and shopping vocabulary; prepositions. Students taking French I will read short novels and write short compositions.

courses.description: This course is a continuation of French I. Students can expect to listen, speak, read and write within a broad cultural context. The student should also expect to engage in daily conversation in the target language. Awareness, understanding and respect of other cultures and their diversity are an integral part of this course. Skills to be acquired include: understand syntax of present and past tenses; use object pronouns; understand syntax of imperative sentences; express frequency; sequence. Vocabulary: health; sports; hobbies; technology; prepositions. Students taking French II will read short novels and write compositions.

courses.description: This semester-long course is an introduction to the Spanish language as it is currently used in the Americas and throughout the world. Students will learn to speak, listen, read, write and present in Spanish. We use a variety of source material including Spanish language news, articles, movies and television shows. Awareness, understanding and respect of other cultures and their diversity are important parts of this course. Students will also learn the basic customs, traditions and culture of Mexico. Projects will include designing comic strips, slide shows, infographics and movies. Students will have the option to take the National Spanish exam, Level 1 in the spring. Skills in Spanish 1: how to conjugate verbs in the present tense; understand adjective agreement, write grammatically correct simple and compound sentences, how to respond to basic questions; make comparisons, and do short presentations for classmates. Using the Descubre 1 textbook, students will learn: introductions; greetings; basic courtesies; classroom and school words; classes; family words; pastimes and hobbies; numbers; all aspects of student and family life including sports, activities. Students taking Spanish have the opportunity to participate in cultural projects and holidays, learn traditional songs, create cultural art pieces, and cook Hispanic food.

courses.description: This semester-long course is a continuation of Spanish I, and completes a full complement of Advanced Novice language learning. Students can expect to listen, speak, read, write and present with more complexity than Spanish 1. Students will engage in daily conversations in Spanish. Students will continue to use authentic, primary source materials including more complex sources online. We continue to add to our knowledge of traditions, customs and cultural aspects of Mexico. Projects include designing infographics, slideshows, movies and stories in Spanish. Students will have the option to take the National Spanish exam, Level 2. Skills in Spanish 2: Continuing in the Descubre 1 book, students will learn: pastimes and hobbies; months, weather and seasons; making plans; household routines; personal routines; and traveling. Students will learn the full range of present tense verbs, as well as using multiple verbs and adjectives. Students taking Spanish 2 have the opportunity to participate in cultural art projects and holidays, learn traditional songs, prepare a meal for the community, and create cultural art projects. Students in Spanish 2 have the opportunity for international travel.

Students use desktop publishing and computer graphics, develop skills in photojournalism, writing and editing, and apply business and management techniques. The creative skills include brainstorming ideas for design, layout and presentation from both the overall design to the individual pages; copywriting and digital photography. courses.description: This dynamic, hands-on course offers students an inside look at the world of media production as they collaboratively plan, film, star in, and edit LRTV every day. Students will gain firsthand experience with studio equipment while tackling both creative and technical roles - developing story ideas, drafting scripts and shot lists, acting, directing, camera operation, lighting, sound, editing and more! The course emphasizes real-world skills like improvisation, problem-solving, teamwork, and learning through experience. Students should expect frequent on-camera roles requiring strong reading, memory and presentation abilities. Course projects ranging from commercials to short films will populate portfolios aimed to impress prospective colleges and employers seeking the next generation of artistic yet technically-savvy video producers.

Through intensive pre-production development, students will write treatments and scripts, storyboard complex camera work and scene sequencing, and explore lighting techniques. Students will work with sophisticated camera and lighting gear as well as personal cell phones to shoot inventive short films, dynamic music videos, compelling documentaries or eye-catching motion graphic projects. For those seeking to elevate their creative perspectives and technical video production prowess, this course unlocks a new world of possibility.
